thread.title: The Comast-Disney Bidding War Over Fox Will Reach Nosebleed Levels

author: Jonathan Berr
title: The Comast-Disney Bidding War Over Fox Will Reach Nosebleed Levels
text:
Walt Disney is expected to add a cash component to its all-stock $52 billion offer for the 21st Century Fox assets being unloaded by Media Mogul Rupert Murdoch including its stake in the Hulu streaming service, the 20th Century Fox studio along with the FX and National Geographic cable channels as it tries to fend off a rival bid from Comcast, according to CNBC . The exact amount of cash that Disney planned to add and the timing of the counter-offer wasn’t clear though there is little doubt that it will happen. Philadelphia-based Comcast last week made an unsolicited $65 billion all-cash offer for the Fox assets, raising expectations of a bidding war. Officials from Disney, whose media properties include the ESPN and Freeform cable networks along the Star Wars film franchise, couldn't be reached for comment. Fox is expected to discuss the Comcast offer at a board meeting Wednesday, media reports said.
When Fox’s stake in the U.K.-based Pay TV service Sky, which is being sold separately, is considered Walt Disney and Comcast likely will spend more than $100 billion on the Fox assets. Comast’s offer for Sky values the company at roughly $31 billion, roughly $4.2 higher than an earlier Disney bid. Both companies are counting on Sky to bolster their overseas operations. Combined, the Sky and Fox deals would be among the largest corporate transactions in history.
It’s anyone’s guess how high the bidding war will get. Both Comcast CEO Brian Roberts and his counterpart at Disney Bob Iger are motivated buyers because assets like Fox’s don’t come on the market very often. Rating agencies have already raised concerns about the level of debt that Comcast and Disney are willing to a take on from the Fox deal. However, Comcast and Disney are fighting for the keys to a shrinking kingdom.
Larger rivals such as Apple (AAPL), which last week signed a development deal with Oprah Winfrey, Facebook and Amazon.com are expanding their foothold in the business of creating and distributing video content. Streaming services such as Netflix and Hulu are also continuing to gain viewers at the expense of so-called linear broadcast and cable networks.
“The irony is that Amazon advertises on the big networks, said Hal Vogel, an independent economist who follows the entertainment industry, in an interview. “(They are) changing the whole structure of the business at the foundation. It’s non-linear. It’s viewing on demand. It’s over-the-top.”
Both Magna Global and Zenith Media noted that the Internet overtook television in 2017 on a global basis to become the world’s dominant advertising medium. TV won't get its title anytime soon if ever.
eMarketer expects U.S. spending on TV to fall 0.5 percent this year to $69.8 billion, equaling about 31.6 percent of total ad spending. Though TV ad purchases will rise again in 2020 for the Olympics and U.S. presidential election, they are expected to drop in subsequent years reaching less than 25 percent of spending by 2022, according to eMarketer. Meanwhile, the growth in fees paid to carry broadcast and cable channels, which have been a cash cow, is slowing. MoffettNathanson earlier this year forecasted basic cable affiliate fees will rise an average of 5 percent from 2015 to 2020, down from an earlier projection of 7.4 percent.
